newsitem.title: USA: Political minefield awaits Gore in China.
newsitem.headline: Political minefield awaits Gore in China.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore's upcoming visit to China has turned into a high-stakes walk through a diplomatic and political minefield created of allegations that China tried to influence U.S. elections.
The overriding goal of Gore's eight-day Asian tour, which begins on Saturday and also includes stops in Japan and South Korea, is to improve volatile U.S.-Sino relations.
He will be the highest-ranking American official to visit China since its military crushed pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.

But the timing of the trip, expected to lay the groundwork for a state visit to Washington by Chinese President Jiang Zemin later this year and a trip to Bejing by U.S. President Bill Clinton in 1998, is politically awkward for Gore.

Congressional investigators and the Justice Department have been looking into allegations that China tried to influence the outcome of last year's presidential election and some races for Congress by secretly making campaign donations -- a breach of U.S. law.
Gore intends to raise the subject during his trip, according to officials but they said it was not expected to become a focal point of the exchanges.

Although Beijing has vigorously denied the charges, the mere hint of scandal complicates Gore's mission. His advisers worry that if he appears too willing to compromise with Beijing, some will read that as influence-buying by China.

"I was frankly a little surprised that Gore went forward with it (the trip), given how this fundraising political influence scandal seems to grow and look more politically ugly as the days pass," said Greg Mastel, an expert on China for the Economic Strategy Institute.
But any delay in the trip, which was agreed to when Clinton met Ziang briefly last November in the Philippines, would have caused a serious diplomatic tiff.
"There's not much he (Gore) could do, but it is a political minefield," Mastel said.

The fundraising charges come at a time when both sides are trying desperately to improve relations from the tense period a year ago when Beijing and Washington traded warnings over Chinese military exercises near Taiwan.
China wants U.S. backing for its efforts to become a member of the World Trade Organisation. Membership in the trade club would give Chinese goods access to foreign markets at lower tariff rates.
Key Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives introduced legislation on Thursday requiring a Congressional vote on U.S. approval of Beijing's bid to join the WTO.
To emphasise trade ties, China has invited Gore to witness the signing of a huge new order to buy jets made by Boeing Co.

Normally any politician -- especially one as ambitious as Gore, who is expected to run for president in the year 2000 -- would jump at a chance to be part of something that creates jobs and helps the U.S. economy.

The offer, however, prompted intense debate about whether Gore would be hurt by attending such a ceremony given the politically charged climate in Washington, where congressional conservatives want a get-tough approach toward China and hope to deny it most-favoured-nation trade status.

A senior administration official said Gore would attend the ceremony because "our policy is to promote the commerical interest of the United States." But the mere fact the issue was debated underscores the sensitivities of the visit.
Gore also plans talks with Jiang, the hand-picked successor of Deng Xiaoping, who died last month.
"Jiang Zemin is waiting to improve relations with America," said Chen You-Wei, a Chinese expert with the Paul Nitze School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University.

Jiang "is constrained by China's domestic policy, politics and the disputes between the two countries over issues such as human rights, the trade deficit and weapons proliferation in Taiwan," Chen said.

Gore departs Washington on Saturday for talks on Monday in Tokyo, flying to Beijing that night. He will visit South Korea late Friday and visit the Demilitarized Zone separating North and South Korea on Saturday before returning to Washington.
